comments: Accurate paraphrase of the quote, including the hedged cost/availability claim. Frame type as observation fits, and post role as solution is correct. Applicability is context-dependent since it varies by manufacturer. Scope labeled as “cost” is only partial since the claim is also about availability; consider “availability and cost” if that taxonomy is allowed.

Accurate capture of the quote: V-cut depanelization tends to leave rounded edges that don't look premium. Frame type as observation and post role as solution are appropriate. Applicability as context-dependent (specific to V-cut) is correct. Scope label 'machining_process' is passable but could be better as 'fabrication/depanelization method' or 'edge aesthetics.' Note the aesthetic judgment is subjective, though stated assertively; direct_neutral stance is acceptable.

Main point is clear and mostly faithful, but it narrows the quote’s general statement about manufacturer capabilities/engagement to PCB edge features specifically. Frame type as risk is reasonable (it represents a business constraint that can block action), though it could also be seen as an observation. The scope label “shop_operations” is not a good fit; this is about vendor/sourcing or manufacturer relationship/business practices. Applicability as context-dependent and epistemic stance as direct_neutral are appropriate. Recommend revising scope to something like “vendor_relations/procurement” and, optionally, generalizing the main point slightly to reflect the broader quote.

Accurate distillation of the quote, including the 50k vs 500 example and the rationale about amortizing tooling cost. This is standard manufacturing economics (not tribal). ‘Heuristic’ fits since it’s prescriptive advice on process selection. Applicability is context-dependent because break-even volume varies with part geometry, mold complexity, material, and machine rates. Labels are appropriate.

The quote supports the advice to buy large sheets and have a shop bandsaw them into 3-inch sections, but the main point adds unstated specifics (plastic material, low-volume context, cost reduction, drilling) not present in the quote. Revise the main point to remove material and volume assumptions: e.g., 'Buy large sheets of the chosen material and have a machine shop bandsaw them into 3-inch-wide strips/blanks for subsequent operations.' Consider updating the subject from 'plastic' to 'sheet stock' or 'material blanks.' Scope could also be framed as 'material preparation,' though 'machining_process' is acceptable.

Accurate summary of the quote: low cost and adequate stiffness/drillability of acrylic for the application. The language is clearly tentative. The frame_type is better labeled as heuristic (advice with rationale) rather than observation, since it suggests using acrylic due to cost and properties. Scope as “material” is fine, and applicability being context-dependent is appropriate (depends on part size/thickness and loads).

Accurate and clear summary of the quote; recommendation to determine springback empirically due to simplifying assumptions in analytical models is sound. Frame type (heuristic) and post role (tutorial) fit well, and the hedged stance is appropriate. The scope label “material” is too narrow—springback and the recommendation to test are influenced by process, tooling, geometry, and setup, not just material. Consider changing scope to process/method or general forming process. Applicability is more context-dependent than universal, since in some cases analytical models may suffice.

Accurate textbook beam theory relationship; clear and correct. Frame type and epistemic stance are appropriate; post role as tutorial is plausible. The scope label 'material' is incorrect—this is a mechanics/beam-theory (geometric/kinematic) relationship largely independent of material (under standard assumptions). Applicability as universal within pure bending is appropriate.

The main point accurately restates the quote and is clear. This is standard plastic bending theory, not tribal knowledge. The frame_type would be better as 'heuristic' (modeling assumption) or possibly 'observation' rather than 'principle,' since it doesn't explain causality. Epistemic stance 'tentative_subjective' is reasonable given 'we can assume,' though 'direct_neutral' could also fit in a tutorial context. Scope labeled as 'material' is only partially fitting; it is more about bending mechanics at small radii (geometry/material interaction).

Main point precisely reflects the quoted formula and conditions. Frame type, post role, applicability, and stance are appropriate. The only weak label is Scope: this is not purely a 'material' scope; it depends on both material properties (Re, E) and tube geometry (mean radius r) and the thin-walled assumption. Suggest scope like 'thin-walled tube bending' or 'material + geometry (thin-walled tubes)'. Keep all else.

Accurate and clear definition of k; the added note about ‘over-bend’ is a reasonable interpretation for springback. However, the frame type is better labeled as observation (a definition) rather than principle (no causal mechanism provided). Applicability could arguably be universal within the chosen springback model, not strongly context-dependent.

Main point matches the quote but adds a bit beyond it (performance/life) which, while reasonable, isn't stated. Frame type could be better labeled as a heuristic (selection advice) rather than an observation. Applicability as universal is reasonable since conductivity and erosion resistance are core criteria across EDM electrode choices.

Accurate core claim; the main point adds an unstated rationale ('due to their favorable properties') that isn't in the quote—trim if aiming for strict fidelity. Frame type, post role, and stance are appropriate. Scope as 'tooling' is reasonable though 'materials' could also fit. Applicability as universal is broadly fine given common industry preference, though it's a general preference rather than an absolute.

Accurate capture of the quote: it states lead/solder aren’t typical EDM electrodes and wear resistance would be unknown without trials. Frame type as observation and post role as solution are appropriate. Scope as tooling is reasonable since electrodes are tooling. Applicability marked universal is mostly fine (it reflects standard practice), though one could argue context-dependent since niche use cases could exist. Epistemic stance is direct-neutral; the language is assertive but not absolute.

The quote recommends considering a coolant recycling system when workload makes automation practical and manual checking impractical. The main point slightly overstates this as “choose” rather than “consider,” but otherwise aligns. Frame type (heuristic) and post role (solution) are appropriate. Scope is reasonable. Applicability should be context_dependent, not universal, since the advice is conditioned on workload/feasibility of automation. Suggest softening the main point’s verb to “consider” and changing Applicability to context_dependent.

Good, useful point, but the frame type is better labeled as observation rather than risk; it's a factual limitation/requirement, not a specific failure mode. The main point adds “for coolant condition,” which isn’t explicit in the quote (though likely true given the thread context). Consider revising to: “Inline mixing still requires periodic machine checks—manually or automatically; it does not eliminate monitoring.” Keep Applicability as universal and Post Role as solution.

Main point is accurate but slightly extrapolates the cause (“relying on periodic top-ups”) which isn’t explicitly in the quoted sentence; consider rephrasing to stick to the observed outcome. Applicability should be context_dependent (depends on coolant type, evaporation, contamination, maintenance practices) rather than universal. Scope label “quality” is vague; suggest “coolant maintenance” or “coolant lifecycle.” Frame type (observation) and post role (solution) are appropriate.

Accurate and clear summary of the quote. Classifying as a principle is appropriate because it explains causality (contaminants cause wear/gumming; recycling removes them). Applicability is generally broad but may depend on the specific recycling setup’s capability, hence not a perfect universal. Otherwise labels fit well.

The quote supports using a refractometer to maintain coolant concentration but does not mention a recycling setup; that part is an overreach. Suggest removing “in a recycling setup.” Also, applicability should be context_dependent (works for water‑miscible coolants with refractive index correlation, not universal across all coolants/systems). Scope label “quality” is passable but “process control” or similar would be more precise. Frame type, post role, and epistemic stance are appropriate.

The main point adds a causal rationale (reduced disposal/new coolant costs) and broadens to “vendors” generally, which is not in the quote. Revise to: “A vendor claims the equipment’s payback is typically 6–9 months.” Frame type (observation), post role (solution), scope (cost), and applicability (context-dependent) are appropriate. Consider changing epistemic stance to direct_neutral; “typically” is a mild hedge but not a subjective/personal claim.

Accurate and clear generalization of the quoted experience; classifying as a risk is appropriate. Applicability is context-dependent and stance is direct. The only weak label is scope: 'machine_capability' is not ideal—this is better framed as an equipment/component susceptibility or electrical-noise vulnerability of the PC’s built-in USB port. Consider revising scope to something like 'component_limitation' or 'electrical_environment'.

Accurate that moving the USB connection to a separate add‑in card stopped the disconnects, but the main point adds a causal inference (“more tolerant of disturbance”) that isn’t stated in the quote. Also the quote says “PCI USB‑3 card,” while the main point specifies PCIe—likely correct but not supported verbatim. Recommend revising the main point to: “Using a USB 3.0 add‑in card’s port (instead of a motherboard port) eliminated the disconnects in this case.” Scope label “machine_capability” is not a good fit; suggest something like system_setup, interface/hardware_selection, or workstation_hardware. The tentative stance is appropriate.

The core claim—gears that mesh must have the same tooth size (module/DP) and cannot be made compatible by simply scaling—is accurately captured. However, the added guidance to “change the tooth count while keeping the module consistent” goes beyond the quoted text. Consider trimming that prescriptive addition unless supported elsewhere in the post. Labeling as a heuristic is reasonable (it’s framed as advice), though it could also be seen as a basic design rule/observation. Applicability as universal and stance as direct/neutral are appropriate.

Accurate restatement of the quote and clearly written. Frame type, post role, scope, and stance are appropriate. However, applicability is not universal—this proportional closeness holds when comparing gears of different tooth counts at the same module/standard proportions. If “larger” means uniformly scaling module, the ratio remains similar. Recommend changing Applicability to context_dependent and noting the assumption of standard gear proportions (fixed module/dedendum).

The quote correctly defines module as a ratio of (pitch) diameter to tooth count, but the main point adds that same module ensures compatible meshing, which is an overreach and not supported by the quote. Meshing also depends on matching pressure angle and other standards. Revise the main point to: “Module m is defined as pitch diameter divided by number of teeth (mm per tooth); gears with the same module have the same tooth size,” optionally noting meshing requires other parameters (e.g., pressure angle) to match. Labels are appropriate; scope and applicability are universal for the definition.

Accurate, clear definitional content. Minor mismatch: the quote mentions a difference in pitch circle diameter, whereas addendum/dedendum are conventionally radial distances from the pitch circle to tip/root. The main point correctly states the radial interpretation and the whole-depth relationship. Labels (observation, solution, universal, direct_neutral) are appropriate.
